messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: HVAC Technician
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 59

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Overanalysing: I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Marco

Marco was twenty-two when he accidentally drove the nail gun through his coworker's leg. It was a Tuesday morning in April, unremarkable except for what happened in the span of three seconds. They were framing a residential addition in Albuquerque, and Marco had been running the gun along the top plate, moving fast because the foreman was pushing to stay on schedule. His coworker, Javier, had stepped into the space where Marco was working—Marco didn't see him, or rather, Marco's mind didn't register him until the sound came: not the usual pneumatic pop of the gun, but a different sound, wet and wrong, followed by Javier's scream. The nail had gone through the meat of his thigh, and for a moment Marco couldn't move. He could smell the heat from the compressor, the acrid metallic tang of the nail gun's exhaust, the sharp copper scent of blood. Javier was on the ground, and Marco was standing above him holding the gun, and everyone was shouting. Javier spent two weeks in the hospital. He recovered, mostly. But Marco did not.

In the months that followed, Marco came to believe that he was fundamentally unreliable—not just careless, but broken in some essential way. His own body had betrayed both him and Javier. His hands, which he had always trusted to do their work, had become instruments of harm. He couldn't look at them without feeling a surge of disgust and dread. What frightened him most was the thought that he might do something like that again, that some part of him was incapable of the basic attention required to keep other people safe. He had not done enough to stop what happened; he had been careless, inattentive, and now he was a person who hurt people. This conviction—that he was unrecognizable to himself, that the careful, responsible person he'd believed he was had never existed—drove him to withdraw from almost everything. He stopped going to job sites. He stopped answering calls from his crew. He told his mother he was sick, and after a while, the lies became easier than the truth. He couldn't bear the thought of being around people who might depend on him, people he might accidentally harm. Staying home felt like the only ethical choice.

But staying home meant avoiding anything that could trigger the memory, which meant avoiding almost everything. He couldn't watch certain movies, couldn't listen to certain songs, couldn't be in hardware stores or anywhere near pneumatic tools. He started keeping a list—not written down, but catalogued in his mind—of all the things that felt dangerous. Loud noises made him flinch. The smell of metal or oil could send him spiraling. He began to structure his days around avoidance: he would only leave the house to buy groceries at a specific store, at a specific time, when he knew it would be quiet. He avoided anniversaries of the accident with ritualistic precision, calling in sick on that date every month, though no one had asked him to. He overanalyzed the event constantly, replaying those three seconds again and again, trying to find the moment where he could have prevented it, the split-second decision he could have unmade. If only he'd been standing two feet to the left. If only he'd looked over his shoulder. If only, if only. But the overanalysis never brought resolution—it only deepened his conviction that he was someone who couldn't be trusted.

The memory itself had taken on a strange quality. When it surfaced—and it surfaced constantly, without warning, forcing its way into his mind at odd moments—it felt like it was happening to someone else. He could see himself holding the gun, could see Javier falling, but the person in that memory didn't feel like him. It was as though he were watching a video of a stranger committing an unforgivable act. Yet the memory was also viscerally present: he could smell the compressor heat, the blood, the metal. His body would react before his mind could catch up—his heart would race, his hands would shake, sweat would break out on his palms. The physical reactivity was immediate and overwhelming, a betrayal by the very body he had come to distrust. And because the memory was so intrusive, so uncontrollable, he found himself increasingly confined to the few places where he felt safe: his bedroom, his mother's kitchen, the backyard where he could see all approaches. Anywhere else felt dangerous, not because of any logical threat, but because the memory could ambush him there, and he couldn't predict or control what his body might do in response.

The silence was the worst part. When things were quiet—when there were no external stimuli to distract him—the memory was most likely to surface. He had come to believe that unusual silence meant something dangerous was about to happen, that the quiet itself was a warning. He started playing music constantly, leaving the television on even when he wasn't watching it, anything to fill the void where the memory might emerge. His mother found him one afternoon sitting in the dark with the radio on, unable to articulate why he couldn't turn it off. He was trapped in a cycle he couldn't name: his conviction that he was untrustworthy made him avoid situations where he might be tested; his avoidance meant he never had the chance to disconfirm that belief. The memory remained intrusive and unprocessed, triggering the physical fear responses that kept him confined to his safe zones, which in turn left him alone with the silence and the smell-memories and the grinding, endless loop of self-recrimination. He had been out of work for eight months when he finally called a therapist. He was terrified that talking about it would make it worse, but he was more terrified of spending the rest of his life imprisoned in four rooms, waiting for the memory to strike.
